messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Piezo source: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and $R_{leak}$ (20M$\Omega$).
    *   Open circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p) \approx 3.2\text{V}$ (nominal).
    *   Requirements:
        *   $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$
    *   Constraints: Max 16 components, max 4 switches, max 2 SYNCs.
    *   Reference (FBR):
        *   S1: OK except settled.
        *   S2 (Heavy load): Fails $V_{avg}$ (1.76V < 1.8V) and $t_{up}$.
        *   S3 (Strong excitation, light load): Fails $V_{max}$ (5.68V > 3.6V) and $V_{pp}$ (84.4mV > 50mV).
        *   S4 (Weak excitation): Fails $V_{avg}$ (1.51V < 1.8V) and $t_{up}$.
        *   S5 (Low freq): Fails settled.
        *   S6: OK.

    *   *Low voltage issues (S2, S4):* Diode drops in a full-bridge (FBR) are significant when $V_{oc}$ is low (3.2V). Using a Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI) or a synchronized switch circuit can flip the voltage across $C_p$, effectively boosting the voltage available for rectification.
    *   *Overvoltage issues (S3):* S3 has a light load and high excitation, leading to $V_{out}$ climbing too high. A Zener clamp (DZ33) is needed to keep $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$.
    *   *Ripple issues (S3):* $V_{pp}$ is high. A larger storage capacitor $C_{out}$ is needed.
    *   *Settling issues (S1, S5):* Likely due to the capacitor size or the interaction between the rectifier and the load. $dv$ needs to be small, meaning the system should reach steady state quickly or have very little drift.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor) with Full-Bridge Rectifier.**
        *   SSHI flips the voltage on $C_p$ at the peaks of the displacement/current, significantly increasing the extracted power and the voltage across the rectifier.
        *   Topology: Inductor $L$ switched across the piezo terminals at the voltage peaks.
        *   Rectification: Full-bridge (DSCH).
        *   Clamping: DZ33 on "out".
        *   Storage: $C_{out}$ on "out".
        *   *Wait*, SSHI typically uses a switch across the piezo. Let's refine the SSHI structure:
            *   Piezo is between `pzp` and `pzn`.
            *   Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in series, connected in parallel with the piezo? Or more traditionally, the switch flips the voltage.
            *   Standard SSHI: $L$ is connected between `pzp` and `pzn` via a switch. When the switch closes, the energy in $C_p$ is transferred to $L$ and then back to $C_p$ with opposite polarity.
            *   Wait, for energy *harvesting*, the SSHI flips the piezo voltage, then the energy is extracted via a rectifier.
            *   Connectivity: Piezo (`pzp`, `pzn`). Switch $S$ and inductor $L$ in series between `pzp` and `pzn`. Rectifier (Full-bridge) from `pzp`/`pzn` to `out`.
            *   Wait, if the rectifier is always connected, the switch $S$ is just flipping $C_p$ against the rectifier. This might not be efficient.
            *   Correction: The "standard" simple SSHI for low-voltage piezo is often a "Parallel SSHI" or "Series SSHI". For a current source model, the inductor-switch combo should flip the charge on $C_p$.

    *   **Design 2: Half-Bridge Rectifier with an active flip (Simplified SSHI/SECE).**
        *   If the piezo is floating (pzp, pzn), we can use a full bridge.
        *   Let's try a simpler approach: Full-bridge + Zener + Large $C_{out}$, and see if adding a switching inductor improves the low-power cases.

    *   **Design 3: SSHI-like structure (Inductor-based voltage inversion).**
        *   Components:
            *   L1: `pzp` to `n1`
            *   S1: `n1` to `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
            *   G1: `edges: both`, `ton: pi*sqrt(L*Cp)`, `phase: 0`. (At the peaks of the voltage, which are the zero-crossings of the current source).
            *   Rectifier:
                *   D1: `pzp` to `out`
                *   D2: `pzn` to `out`
                *   D3: `0` to `pzp`
                *   D4: `0` to `pzn`
            *   Storage: C1: `out` to `0`
            *   Clamp: DZ1: `0` to `out` (DZ33)

    *   *S2/S4 (Voltage too low):* SSHI should increase the average voltage by effectively increasing the voltage swing across the diodes.
    *   *S3 (Voltage too high):* DZ33 Zener clamp will limit $V_{out}$ to $\sim 3.3\text{V}$.
    *   *S3 (Ripple):* Large $C_{out}$ (e.g., $4.7\mu\text{F}$) will reduce $V_{pp}$.
    *   *Startup/Settling:* Higher efficiency from SSHI helps $t_{up}$. Large $C_{out}$ might slow down $t_{up}$, so we need to balance it.

    *   Wait, the reference FBR failed S2 and S4. $V_{oc}$ is $3.2\text{V}$. Rectifier drop is $\sim 0.5\text{V}$. $3.2 - 0.5 = 2.7\text{V}$. Why did it fail?
        *   S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega$. $I_{load} = 1.8\text{V} / 150\text{k}\Omega = 12\mu\text{A}$.
        *   S4: $R_L = 1\text{M}\Omega$. $I_{load} = 1.8\text{V} / 1\text{M}\Omega = 1.8\mu\text{A}$.
        *   The issue is likely that the piezo is a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$. The energy per cycle is $\int I^2 R dt$.
        *   With $C_p$, the voltage is $V = \frac{1}{C_p} \int I dt$.
        *   $V_{peak} = I_p / (\omega C_p)$. For S4: $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}$, $\omega = 2\pi \cdot 100$, $C_p = 25\text{nF} \implies V_{peak} = 30\mu / (628 \cdot 25\text{n}) = 1.91\text{V}$.
        *   If $V_{peak}$ is only $1.91\text{V}$, then $V_{peak} - 2 \cdot V_{diode} \approx 1.91 - 0.5 = 1.41\text{V}$.
        *   This is below $1.8\text{V}$! This is why FBR fails S4 and S2.
        *   *Crucial insight:* We MUST use a voltage-boosting technique (like SSHI) because the open-circuit voltage peak is actually quite low in some conditions (S4).

    *   The goal is to flip the charge on $C_p$ to avoid it canceling itself out and to build up voltage.
    *   In SSHI, the switch closes at the voltage peaks.
    *   Let's refine the components:
        *   S1: `pzp` to `pzn` via $L1$.
        *   $L1$: `pzp` to `n1`.
        *   $S1$: `n1` to `pzn`.
        *   G1: `edges: both`, `ton: 30us` (approx $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$ for $L=1\text{mH}, C_p=25\text{nF} \implies \pi \sqrt{25 \cdot 10^{-12}} \approx 15\mu\text{s}$. Let's use $20\text{-}30\mu\text{s}$).
        *   Now the rectifier:
            *   If we use a full bridge, we are extracting energy.
            *   Wait, if the switch is in parallel with the piezo, it will flip the voltage. But the rectifier is also in parallel. The rectifier will try to clamp the voltage.
            *   Standard SSHI usually has the switch and inductor in *series* with the piezo, or it uses a specific configuration.
            *   Actually, for the "Parallel SSHI", the rectifier is connected to the piezo, and the switch/inductor is also connected in parallel. The switch closes at the voltage peaks.
            *   Is this correct? Let's check. If $V_{pzp}$ is at a peak, closing $S1$ creates an LC oscillation between $L1$ and $C_p$, flipping the voltage to $-V_{peak}$. This effectively doubles the voltage swing.

    *   Wait, if the switch is in parallel, does it fight the rectifier?
        *   At the peak, $V_{pzp}$ is high. The rectifier's diode $D1$ is conducting. If we close $S1$, the inductor $L1$ will draw current from $C_p$. The rectifier diode $D1$ is still forward-biased, but the inductor is now in parallel.
        *   Actually, a better SSHI for this would be to have the rectifier *after* the SSHI flip, but the simplest implementation is the Parallel SSHI.

    *   *Alternative:* A Charge Pump or a Boost Converter? No, those are too complex for 16 components and require a clock. The SYNC controller is specifically designed for SSHI-like operations (edges: both, ton).

    *   L1: `pzp` to `n1`
    *   S1: `n1` to `pzn`
    *   G1: `edges: both`, `ton: 2e-5`, `phase: 0`
    *   D1: `pzp` to `out` (DSCH)
    *   D2: `pzn` to `out` (DSCH)
    *   D3: `0` to `pzp` (DSCH)
    *   D4: `0` to `pzn` (DSCH)
    *   C1: `out` to `0` (Storage, e.g., 2.2uF)
    *   DZ1: `0` to `out` (DZ33, for S3 overvoltage)

    *   S3: $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. DZ33 clamps it to 3.3V. OK.
    *   S3: $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$. Large $C1$ (e.g., $10\mu\text{F}$) will keep ripple low. OK.
    *   S4: $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$. SSHI will flip the voltage, potentially doubling the effective $V_{oc}$. $1.91\text{V} \cdot 2 = 3.82\text{V}$. $3.82 - 0.5 = 3.32\text{V}$. This is well above 1.8V. OK.
    *   S2: Similar to S4. OK.
    *   S1, S5, S6: Should be OK.
    *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$: SSHI is more efficient, so $t_{up}$ should be fine.
    *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$: Large $C1$ and stabilized voltage should help.

    *   A full bridge has 2 diode drops. A half-bridge (if one terminal is grounded) has 1. But the piezo is a current source between `pzp` and `pzn`, so it's floating. A full bridge is necessary unless we ground `pzn`.
    *   If we ground `pzn`, we lose half the current? No, the current source is $I_p \sin(\omega t)$. If we ground `pzn`, the current still flows through the circuit.
    *   Wait, the piezo model is a current source $I_p \sin(\omega t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ and $R_{leak}$. If we ground `pzn`, the current $I_p$ flows into the circuit and then to ground.
    *   Let's try a half-bridge (D1: `pzp` to `out`, D2: `pzn` to `out` is NOT a half bridge).
    *   A half-bridge would be: D1: `pzp` to `out`, then `pzn` tied to `0`. But $I_p$ is sinusoidal, so it would only harvest half the cycle.
    *   Stick with the Full-Bridge SSHI.

    *   The SYNC controller closes switches at "piezo voltage extrema", which occur at the "zero crossings of the piezo current". This is exactly what's needed for SSHI.
    *   `ton` should be roughly $\pi \sqrt{L C_p}$. For $L=1\text{mH}$ and $C_p=25\text{nF}$, $t = 3.14 \cdot \sqrt{25 \cdot 10^{-12}} = 3.14 \cdot 5 \cdot 10^{-6} \approx 15.7\mu\text{s}$.
    *   Let's propose this SSHI structure.

    *   Wait, can I improve the rectifier? Maybe use a bridge with a capacitor and a Zener.
    *   One more thing: the `dv` (settling) failure in FBR for S1 and S5. This often means the capacitor is too small or the system is oscillating. A larger $C_{out}$ usually helps.

    *   Topology 1: Full-Bridge SSHI (as described).
    *   Topology 2: Full-Bridge with Zener and *very* large $C_{out}$ (just in case the SSHI is too complex or unstable, but the $V_{oc}$ in S4 is so low that FBR is almost guaranteed to fail).
    *   Topology 3: SSHI with a slightly different switch configuration? No, the Parallel SSHI is the most standard. Let's try a "Half-Bridge SSHI" just in case? No, let's stick to the full bridge. Actually, let's try a different approach for the second one: a "Voltage Doubler" (Dickson-like) but those are for DC-DC. For AC, the bridge is the way.

    *   Let's reconsider the SSHI switch:
        *   Inductor $L$ in series with Switch $S$ across the piezo.
        *   Wait, if the bridge is already there, $C_p$ is not just $C_p$, it's $C_p$ in parallel with the diodes. When the diode is conducting, the voltage is clamped to $V_{out} \pm V_d$.
        *   For SSHI to work, the switch must flip the voltage *before* the diode conducts, or the inductor must be strong enough to overcome the clamp.
        *   In a parallel SSHI, the switch is indeed in parallel with the piezo and the rectifier. The switch closes at the voltage peak. Since the voltage is already clamped by the diode, the SSHI flip happens from $V_{out} + V_d$ to $-(V_{out} + V_d)$. This is actually how it's intended to work to boost the voltage.

    *   L1: `pzp`, `n1`
    *   S1: `n1`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
    *   G1: `ton=2e-5`, `phase=0`, `edges=both`
    *   D1: `pzp`, `out` (DSCH)
    *   D2: `pzn`, `out` (DSCH)
    *   D3: `0`, `pzp` (DSCH)
    *   D4: `0`, `pzn` (DSCH)
    *   C1: `out`, `0`
    *   DZ1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)

    *   Is there any other way? A charge pump? Not with these components.
    *   What about a "Synchronous Rectifier"? We have switches and SYNC.
    *   A synchronous rectifier would replace the diodes with switches.
    *   S1: `pzp`, `out`
    *   S2: `pzn`, `out`
    *   S3: `0`, `pzp`
    *   S4: `0`, `pzn`
    *   But we only have 4 switches and 2 SYNCs. We'd need 4 SYNCs to control the 4 switches at different times.
    *   Wait, we can use the same SYNC for two switches if they operate together.
    *   S1 (`pzp`, `out`) and S3 (`0`, `pzn`) would close together.
    *   S2 (`pzn`, `out`) and S4 (`0`, `pzp`) would close together.
    *   This would be a synchronous bridge. It would eliminate the diode drops.
    *   Let's try this as Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectifier.
    *   *Synchronous Bridge:*
        *   G1: `edges: pos`, `ton: 0.005` (half period), `phase: 0`
        *   S1: `pzp`, `out` (ctrl: G1)
        *   S2: `0`, `pzn` (ctrl: G1)
        *   G2: `edges: neg`, `ton: 0.005`, `phase: 0`
        *   S3: `pzn`, `out` (ctrl: G2)
        *   S4: `0`, `pzp` (ctrl: G2)
        *   C1: `out`, `0`
        *   DZ1: `0`, `out` (DZ33)
        *   *Wait*, `ton` for the rectifier should be half the period, but the `ton` limit is $0.001\text{s}$. So synchronous rectification cannot be done with the given `ton` limit (max $1\text{ms}$, while $1/200\text{s} = 5\text{ms}$).
        *   So the synchronous bridge is out.

    *   *Wait*, another topology: "Series SSHI". In Series SSHI, the inductor and switch are in series with the piezo. This is more complex to wire. Let's stick to the Parallel SSHI and maybe a modified FBR.

    *   Actually, let's try a second proposal that is a "Half-Bridge SSHI" just in case the full bridge is too lossy.
        *   Piezo `pzp` and `pzn`.
        *   S1: `pzp`, `pzn` via $L1$.
        *   Rectifier: D1 (`pzp`, `out`), D2 (`pzn`, `out`), D3 (`0`, `pzp`), D4 (`0`, `pzn`). (Wait, that's the same).
        *   What if we use a half-bridge rectifier and ground `pzn`?
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out`
        *   C1: `out`, `0`
        *   `pzn` connected to `0`.
        *   S1: `pzp`, `0` via $L1$.
        *   This would only harvest the positive half-cycle of the current, but the SSHI flip would happen. This is likely less efficient.

    *   Let's use the Parallel SSHI as the main proposal. For the second, let's try a "Filtered FBR with a Zener" but with a very large capacitor and maybe a different diode model for the return path? No, DSCH is already the best.

    *   Actually, let's refine the Parallel SSHI. The inductor value is key. $L=1\text{mH}$ to $10\text{mH}$ is a common range. $C_p = 25\text{nF}$.
    *   Let's provide two versions of the SSHI: one with a full bridge and one with a Zener and a smaller capacitor to see if it affects $t_{up}$. Wait, the evolution strategy will optimize the values. I just need to provide the connectivity.

    *   Wait, I can provide 3 designs.
        1.  Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener Clamp.
        2.  Parallel SSHI + Half Bridge (pzn to 0) + Zener Clamp.
        3.  FBR + Zener Clamp + Large C (this is just an improved FBR).

    *   Wait, let's rethink the "Half Bridge SSHI". If `pzn` is grounded, the current $I_p$ flows into `pzp`. The SSHI switch $S1$ would be between `pzp` and ground.
        *   S1: `pzp`, `n1`
        *   L1: `n1`, `0`
        *   G1: `edges: both`, `ton: 2e-5`, `phase: 0`
        *   D1: `pzp`, `out`
        *   C1: `out`, `0`
        *   DZ1: `0`, `out`
        *   This only works if the piezo is a voltage source. For a current source, the current $I_p$ must return. If `pzn` is grounded, it does. But we only get the positive half-cycle.
        *   Actually, the Parallel SSHI with a Full Bridge is much more robust.

    *   Is there any other way to boost? A "Charge Pump" uses switches and capacitors.
        *   S1: `pzp`, `n1`
        *   C2: `n1`, `out`
        *   S2: `n1`, `out`
        *   This is getting complex and we only have 2 SYNCs.

    *   Let's stick to:
        1.  Parallel SSHI + Full-Bridge Rectifier + Zener Clamp.
        2.  Parallel SSHI + Full-Bridge Rectifier (No Zener, maybe the evolution strategy finds a way? No, S3 needs a clamp).
        3.  A modified FBR with a Zener and a very large $C_{out}$ to see if we can at least pass S1, S2, S5, S6. (Wait, the user wants me to fix *everything*).

    *   Actually, I'll propose the Parallel SSHI in two slightly different ways (maybe one with a different switch location). No, that's the same topology.
    *   How about a "Buck-Boost" inspired SSHI? No, too many components.

    *   Let's refine Proposal 1:
